gaps.sentence: Visitors ___ to leave the gallery by 6 p.m.
gaps.hint: have to takes the full infinitive
gaps.explanation: 'Have to' takes the full infinitive with 'to': have to leave.

gaps.sentence: She ___ have received your email — her inbox was full last week.
gaps.hint: ruled out as a past possibility
gaps.explanation: 'Can't have' plus the participle rules out a past possibility: can't have received.

gaps.sentence: We ___ have hurried — the concert was cancelled anyway.
gaps.hint: the rush turned out to be unnecessary
gaps.explanation: 'Needn't have hurried' means we hurried although it was unnecessary: needn't have.

gaps.sentence: Sorry I am late — I ___ to take my car to the garage this morning.
gaps.explanation: Past obligation uses 'had to', since 'must' has no past form: had to.

gaps.sentence: You ___ better book now — the prices rise every week.
gaps.explanation: 'Had better' gives strong advice, often with urgency: had better book.

gaps.sentence: In this lab, food and drink ___ be brought past the reception area.
gaps.explanation: Written prohibitions use 'must not': must not be brought.

gaps.sentence: You ___ to apply for a visa before you travel; the airline will check it.
gaps.explanation: 'Need to' expresses necessity and, unlike 'must', takes 'to': need to apply.

gaps.sentence: I do not know whose coat this is — it ___ belong to one of the guests.
gaps.explanation: 'Might' hedges a guess when the speaker is not sure: might belong.
